paragraphs: On 4 October 2016, Google introduced the original Pixel and Pixel XL, marking a major pivot away from the developer-focused Nexus line and ushering in what is now a decade of “Made by Google” hardware – but which is best and why?

Over the past 10 years, the lineup has expanded from a pair of traditional slab smartphones to a product portfolio that includes foldable devices, watches, earbuds, a single tablet, and budget-focused A-series models, culminating in the Pixel 11 series.

I’m biased, I think that the 4a is the best of the bunch, but determining which device holds the title of the best Pixel to date is going to be a fun, healthy debate for those of us who have used more than a few of the lineup over the years, especially as not all have been covered in glory.

The original Pixel and Pixel XL established Google’s focus on camera processing and clean software integration. While the launch models lacked water resistance and stereophonic audio, their computational photography capabilities set a new baseline for mobile imaging.

A year later, the Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL introduced the iconic “Panda” design and front-facing stereo speakers. Although the LG-manufactured Pixel 2 XL faced criticism regarding display viewing angles, the series remains highly regarded for solidifying Google’s image processing dominance.

The Pixel 3 and 3 XL introduced Night Sight and a dedicated Pixel Visual Core chip, alongside dual front-facing cameras with an ultra-wide sensor. Despite memory management limits tied to its 4GB of RAM and the prominent display notch on the XL model, the third-generation devices brought significant refinements to software performance. Shortly after, the Pixel 3a series created the mid-range budget category for Google, pairing flagship camera capabilities with lower price points.

Google shifted its approach with the Pixel 4 and 4 XL, introducing Soli radar gesture controls, 90Hz Motion Sense displays, and the only instance of 3D Face Unlock. The removal of the rear fingerprint scanner and poor battery life on the smaller model limited its appeal, though the 4 XL maintains a loyal following for its build, slim profile, and biometric features.

The 4a and 4a 5G focused back on value during a period of transition. That path culminated in the Pixel 5, which abandoned high-end flagship processors in favor of a mid-range Qualcomm Snapdragon 765G chipset, a uniform-bezel design, a rear fingerprint sensor, and a high-density battery. The Pixel 5a with 5G followed a similar template with a larger form factor and water resistance.
